exercises.prompt:
How many bytes does this record take with the default `USAGE DISPLAY`? (GnuCOBOL's `FUNCTION LENGTH(rec)` prints the answer.)

```cobol
01 rec.
   05 a PIC X(3).
   05 b PIC 9(4)V99.
   05 c PIC S9(3).
```

feedback.message: Not yet: one of `V` and `S` takes no position. In fact neither does here.
Not yet: `V` is an implied point and is not stored, and with `DISPLAY` usage the sign of `S9(3)` shares a byte with a digit.

exercises.solution: `a` is 3 bytes, `b` is 4 + 2 = 6 digits (the `V` is not stored), and `c` is 3 digits with the sign held in the same bytes. 3 + 6 + 3 = **12**, which is what `FUNCTION LENGTH(rec)` prints.

exercises.prompt:
What does this fragment print?

```cobol
01 city PIC X(8).
...
    MOVE "Johannesburg" TO city
    DISPLAY "[" city "]"
```
hints: An alphanumeric receiver is filled from the left.
Which end is cut off when the value is too long?
exercises.solution: Text is placed from the left and cut off on the right when it does not fit, so only the first eight characters survive: **`[Johannes]`**. No error or warning is raised at run time.

exercises.prompt:
With GnuCOBOL, what does this fragment print?

```cobol
01 small-amt PIC 9(3)V99.
...
    MOVE 98765.4321 TO small-amt
    DISPLAY "[" small-amt "]"
```

feedback.message: Not yet: `MOVE` truncates extra decimal places; it does not round.
Not yet: numbers are aligned on the decimal point, not on the left.

hints: Line the value up on its decimal point.
Keep three digits before the point and two after; drop the rest.
exercises.solution: A numeric move aligns on the decimal point, then keeps the three integer digits nearest the point (`765`) and the first two decimals (`43`). The `98` on the left and the `21` on the right are dropped. GnuCOBOL displays the implied point, so the output is **`[765.43]`**.

exercises.prompt:
What does this fragment print? Type the brackets and spaces exactly.

```cobol
01 signed-out PIC ---9.99.
...
    MOVE -3.5 TO signed-out
    DISPLAY "[" signed-out "]"
```
hints: The picture has seven positions: three `-`, a `9`, a point and two `9`s.
A floating minus moves to just before the first significant digit.
exercises.solution: The picture is seven characters wide. The value is 3.50, so the integer part needs only the `9` position. The three `-` symbols float: the leftmost ones become spaces, and one becomes the minus sign right before the `3`. The result is **`[  -3.50]`** (two spaces, then `-3.50`).

exercises.prompt: An account balance can be anything from −9,999,999.99 to 9,999,999.99. Which picture should hold it for arithmetic?

options.label: `PIC S9(7)V99`
options.feedback: Yes: signed, seven integer digits, two decimals, nine bytes in `DISPLAY` usage.

options.label: `PIC 9(7)V99`
options.feedback: Not yet. Without `S`, a negative balance loses its sign as soon as it is stored.

options.label: `PIC -Z,ZZZ,ZZ9.99`
options.feedback: Not yet. That is an edited picture, fine for printing the balance but not usable in arithmetic.

options.label: `PIC X(12)`
options.feedback: Not yet. Text cannot take part in arithmetic, and nothing would stop letters getting in.

hints: You need a sign, and you need to compute with it.
exercises.solution: **`S9(7)V99`**. `S` keeps the sign, `9(7)` covers up to 9,999,999, and `V99` gives two decimal places. Edited pictures are only for output: keep the value here and move it to `-Z,ZZZ,ZZ9.99` when printing.

exercises.prompt: A statement printer moves a refund of −250.00 into `PIC ZZ,ZZ9.99` and prints it. What appears?

options.label: `   250.00`, which looks like a charge
options.feedback: Yes. A picture made only of `Z`, `9`, `,` and `.` has nowhere to put a sign, so it is silently dropped.
Not yet. There is no `-`, `+`, `CR` or `DB` in the picture, so no sign can appear.

options.label: A run-time error, because the value is negative
options.feedback: Not yet. `MOVE` never raises an error for this; it does what the picture allows.
Not yet. Asterisks come only from the `*` symbol.

hints: Look for a symbol in the picture that could show a sign.
exercises.solution: The picture has no sign position, so the minus is lost and the refund prints as **`   250.00`**. Use `-ZZ,ZZ9.99`, `--,--9.99` or `ZZ,ZZ9.99CR` for any amount that can be negative.

exercises.prompt: A record has `05 qty PIC 9(3).` and `05 name PIC X(10).` A colleague clears it with `MOVE SPACES TO the-record` and later runs `ADD 1 TO qty`. What is the best explanation of the risk?

options.label: A group move copies characters without looking at the fields, so `qty` now holds spaces, which is not valid numeric data; on IBM mainframes the ADD can stop the program with a data exception (S0C7).
options.feedback: Yes. Use `INITIALIZE the-record`, which sets numeric fields to zero and alphanumeric fields to spaces.

options.label: There is no risk: `MOVE SPACES` sets numeric fields to zero automatically.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what `INITIALIZE` does. A move to a group is a plain character copy.

options.label: The compiler will reject `MOVE SPACES` to a group containing numeric fields.
options.feedback: Not yet. It is perfectly legal, which is exactly why it is a trap.

options.label: `name` will be filled with zeros.
options.feedback: Not yet. `name` gets spaces, which is fine; the problem is `qty`.

hints: Does a move to a group item know about the fields inside it?
exercises.solution: A move to a group item is an alphanumeric move of the whole record, so every byte becomes a space, including the three bytes of `qty`. Arithmetic on non-numeric data is invalid; IBM mainframes report it as a data exception (abend **S0C7**). `INITIALIZE` is the safe way to reset a record.
